name: Wendy Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week depends on the season. In summer it's weddings, sometimes three on a Saturday, hauling a forty-kilo harp on a trolley up church steps. Twice a week I play for afternoon tea at a country hotel, and I teach six harp pupils in our front room. I also record gentle harp pieces for a sleep app, which pays a little each month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does it all fit together, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tightly. My concert harp is on a payment plan, a hundred and forty a month for another three years, and that comes before almost anything. I live with my fiancé Tom, who's an electrician, and we're getting married next August, so every spare penny goes to that. We go to church most Sundays, and I play there for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people value real music when it matters. I'd say it to the brides I meet and to the vicar. I wouldn't post much; I mostly use social media for wedding photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a little AI hurts the sleep app money. They've already started adding generated tracks, and my monthly payment fell from ninety to about fifty. Even if AI changes nothing else, a sleep app full of computer harp music has already halved my steadiest little cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more effort into funerals, which happen all year, by visiting the three funeral directors in town with a card and a recording. I'd ask the hotel for a third afternoon. And I'd keep using the AI writing helper for wedding enquiry emails, which Tom showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little anxious, mostly because of the harp payments and the wedding. Not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a summer's quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Tom covers more of the rent and I feel awful. Two summers ago I only did nine weddings instead of twenty, because of a wet season and a lot of cancellations. I ate into the savings and they've never really recovered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wedding, a bit, which is sad to say. We'd go from a hundred guests to sixty. The harp payment I can't cut, because if I miss two they take it back.

say: People **value real music** when it matters most.
I'd tell **brides and the vicar**, rather than post online.
think: The **sleep app** payment has already dropped from ninety to fifty.
The **harp payments** and our wedding are my real pressure.
do: Visit the town's three **funeral directors** with a card and recording.
Ask the hotel for a **third afternoon** a week.
Keep using the **AI writing helper** for enquiry emails.
feel: A little **anxious**, mostly about the **harp payments**.
S0.quote: Even if AI changes nothing else, a sleep app full of computer harp music has already halved my steadiest little cheque.
fieldNote: AI already cuts her **app income**, even in AI Plateau.
A wet summer once cut her weddings from **twenty to nine**.
She'd **shrink her own wedding** before missing a harp payment.

steps.text: Visit the three funeral directors in town with a card and recording
Ask the country hotel for a third afternoon-tea session
Use the AI writing helper for wedding enquiry emails
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a wedding is the one day people want everything real, and a harpist is part of that. I'd tell my pupils' parents that learning an instrument builds character. I'd keep it positive, because brides don't book a worried harpist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the sleep app work goes completely, and the hotel might swap me for a speaker playing generated harp. Weddings and funerals stay, because they're about being there. A woman getting married wants a harpist walking her down the aisle, but a country hotel's afternoon tea can manage with a speaker in the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the sleep app recording and put that time into weddings and funerals, maybe with a simple website and the AI booking tools other musicians use. I'd look for two more pupils through church. And Tom and I would put an extra fifty a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It feels like weather, something you prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the AI booking tools other musicians use. Would you trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a friend had used one for a season and it hadn't double-booked her, yes. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last either. Tom would set it up and I'd check it every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help musicians through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ourselves first, and our families and churches. I don't expect the government to pay me to play the harp. If anything, I'd like them to keep taxes low on small businesses like mine.

say: A wedding is the day people want **everything real**.
Brides don't book a **worried harpist**, so I'd keep it positive.
think: The **sleep app** work goes completely, and soon.
The hotel could swap me for a **speaker** in the corner playing generated harp.
do: Stop app recording and focus on **weddings and funerals**.
Set up an **AI booking** website once a friend proves it.
Put an **extra fifty** a month aside with Tom.
S1.quote: A woman getting married wants a harpist walking her down the aisle, but a country hotel's afternoon tea can manage with a speaker in the corner.
fieldNote: She splits her work into **being there** jobs and background jobs.

She wants **low taxes**, not support, for small businesses like hers.

steps.text: Stop recording for the sleep app and focus on weddings and funerals
Set up an AI booking website once a friend has tested it
Put an extra fifty a month aside with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to pull together, and churches will matter more than ever. I'd say it to the congregation and to my pupils' parents. I'd also say people shouldn't panic-sell their homes or instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and the thinking side is gone, and I'd guess a lot of the people who'd pay for a harpist at their wedding lose their office jobs. Tom's electrical work is hands-on, so he'd have until about 2031. My fiancé Tom's hands would keep us fed until 2031, but my harp might not survive the first year of everyone losing their office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the harp company about handing the concert harp back and getting a smaller lever harp, which is cheaper and lighter. I'd make our wedding small, at church with a tea in the hall afterwards, maybe this spring instead of next August. And I'd ask Tom's boss whether there's labouring work as his mate, even part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A cold feeling in the stomach, mostly about the harp, oddly, because it's the thing I've worked hardest for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd bring the wedding forward. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything's going to be uncertain, I'd rather be married to Tom while it happens. My mum and dad married in a recession, and they always said it made them a team. It's the one thing I'd be sure of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that change things for Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me more for him than for me, in a way. By 2031 a robot might be wiring houses. But that's three years of his wage, and in three years we'd have worked something else out, I hope.

say: Families need to **pull together**, and churches will matter more.
People shouldn't **panic-sell** their homes or instruments in the first rush.
think: The people who'd book a harpist lose their **office jobs**.
Tom's **hands-on** wage would carry us until about 2031.
do: Swap the concert harp for a cheaper **lever harp**.
Bring our **wedding forward** to spring, small, at church.
Ask Tom's boss about **labouring work** as his mate.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a **cold feeling** about losing the harp.
S2.quote: My fiancé Tom's hands would keep us fed until 2031, but my harp might not survive the first year of everyone losing their office jobs.
fieldNote: Her **fiancé Tom's** trade makes him the household's anchor here.
She'd **marry sooner**, following her parents' recession wedding.
Giving up the **concert harp** would hurt most, as her biggest achievement.

steps.text: Hand back the concert harp and switch to a cheaper lever harp
Bring the wedding forward to spring with a church-hall tea
Ask Tom's boss about part-time labouring work
Lean on church and family through the change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and sensible people will use it. I'd tell young musicians to learn something practical alongside their instrument. At church I'd say we should be ready to help families who get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the app and hotel work fade, and the weddings start thinning as people lose office jobs around 2031. Tom's fine until about 2034. Five years is enough time for me to stop being a harpist who needs weddings and become a harp teacher who needs children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up teaching, aiming for fifteen pupils, and offer harp at two local schools as an extra. I'd do a short teaching course, about three hundred, once I'd seen it help someone I know. I'd keep paying off the harp, because in three years it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. I like having a few years to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tom and the wedding: does that change in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the date next August, but smaller, about seventy guests. Then we'd try for a baby a year or so after, like we planned. Five years feels just about enough time to be sensible about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the dull bits, probably, like booking lessons and reminders. I'd want a person teaching the harp, though, because so much of it is how you hold your hands. I'd use what other teachers use, not try everything.

say: Five years is **fair warning**, and sensible people will use it.
Young musicians should learn **something practical** alongside their instrument.
think: The **app and hotel** work fade first, well before 2031.
Weddings thin out as people lose **office jobs** around 2031.
do: Build up to **fifteen pupils** and offer harp in two schools.

feel: **Anxious** but **hopeful**, with time to do it properly.

fieldNote: She reframes herself as a **harp teacher**, not a wedding harpist.
The five-year window keeps their **wedding and baby** plans roughly intact.

steps.text: Build up to fifteen harp pupils through church and schools

Keep the wedding next August with seventy guests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people who work hard and plan will be fine. I'd encourage families to keep music in their children's lives. At church I'd say look out for the older folk who can't retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be thirty-seven, probably with a child, and the harp paid off long ago. Tom's trade runs till about 2039. With ten years and a husband who wires houses, I can be calm about AI, so long as I'm teaching children and not just playing at hotel teas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep things much as they are for a few years and grow the teaching slowly. Once the harp's paid off in three years, I'd buy a small second-hand lever harp for pupils to borrow. And Tom and I would keep our wedding date and our plans for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now and then, mostly calm. It feels like something we can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sleep app and hotel money still going early, before AGI. And not knowing what weddings will look like in 2036. But Tom's wage and the pupils feel solid enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this version you'd do differently from your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents never saved, and they were always fine, until they weren't. I'd want Tom and me to have three months put by before the baby comes. That would be a first for me.

say: People who **work hard and plan** will be fine with ten years.
We should look out for **older folk** who can't retrain.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven**, with the harp long paid off.
Teaching children and Tom's trade make the household feel **solid enough**.
do: Grow the **teaching** slowly over a few years.
Buy a second-hand **lever harp** for pupils once the main harp is paid.
Save **three months** of costs before a baby comes.
S4.quote: With ten years and a husband who wires houses, I can be calm about AI, so long as I'm teaching children and not just playing at hotel teas.
fieldNote: Tom's **trade** and her growing pupil list make her uneasy rather than anxious.
Her **app and hotel** income still goes early, before AGI.

steps.text: Grow the harp pupil list slowly over the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the people who book harpists would lose their jobs before Tom's trade even gets touched, and I'd lose the harp. What would help is the harp company letting people pause payments, and small businesses paying less tax while they adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about funerals. At a funeral the harp isn't background music; I'm watching the family and slowing down when the widow can't walk any faster.

headlineQuote: At a funeral the harp isn't background music; I'm watching the family and slowing down when the widow can't walk any faster.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old harpist** who plays weddings, funerals and hotel teas, and teaches six pupils.
She lives with her fiancé Tom, an **electrician**, and pays **140 a month** for her harp.
She uses **AI now and then** once proven, often with Tom setting it up.
She trusts **family, church** and hard work over government help.
Across the scenarios she moves from **wedding harpist** to harp teacher, leaning on Tom's trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because harp bookings would collapse before Tom's trade is touched.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** for small businesses while they adapt.
